newsitem.title: BRAZIL: FEATURE - Iconoclastic Brazilian banker on a roll.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Iconoclastic Brazilian banker on a roll.

text.p: Ezequiel Nasser is not a man to waste time.
So in December, when he got the chance to get his Banco Excel Economico's name on the Corinthians soccer club jersey, he didn't hesitate.
In a matter of weeks, Nasser acquired five of Brazil's top soccer players for close to $20 million and transferred them to Sao Paulo to play for the Corinthians, Brazil's second largest soccer club.
But Nasser's master stroke was a clause in the players' contract which required them not only to play on the field, but to star in Excel Economico's ad campaign.
"It was a very daring move. One does not usually associate banks with soccer," was the disapproving remark of the president of a rival Sao Paulo bank.
But it was typical of Nasser, a man who says he is not afraid of breaking the mould, even when it comes to a business as conservative as banking.
"Traditional bankers are demodes," Nasser told Reuters.
His latest drive is to transform Excel Economico into one of Brazil's five top financial institutions within a period of five years.
CRUCIAL PERIOD IN BRAZILIAN BANKING SECTOR
The 52 year-old Nasser has set himself this challenge just as Brazil's banking sector is being rocked by the biggest shakeout in its history.

The success of President Fernando Henrique Cardoso's economic stabilisation plan has eliminated the float, which for many years allowed banks to earn easy and almost risk-free profits. The result has been the abrupt closure of many smaller and less competitive financial institutions.

Meanwhile, lower inflation has also led to an increase in real income for around 35 million Brazilians, who for the first time in their lives are reaching the end of the month with a small amount of money to spare.

It was with an eye on these new low-income consumers that Nasser decided to sponsor the Corinthians. He saw a partnership with a soccer club that has 18 million fans across the country as a golden opportunity to lure new business.
"The deal was very attractive. We want to be a bank of the masses, so we joined forces with a team of the masses," Nasser said.
Building on the success of his Corinthians project, Nasser has since signed sponsorship agreements with two other small regional soccer clubs.
AN UNCONVENTIONAL APPROACH TO BANKING

Nasser's entry into the world of soccer is just the latest of several unconventional strategies introduced by this Syrian-born naturalised Brazilian whose family has been in the banking business for the last three generations.

Last year, he startled Brazil's staid banking community by making a bid for selected assets and liabilities of failed Banco Economico, once the country's eighth largest private bank, which collapsed in 1995 after one of the biggest banking scandals in recent history.

At the time, Nasser's Excel Banco had only six branches and was just a fraction of the size of Banco Economico. Many analysts doubted he would be capable of swallowing the bloated and mismanaged Banco Economico.
But Nasser said he was determined to grow by focusing on retail banking, and said he saw the Banco Economico deal as a way of moving into the big leagues.
"It takes a long time to build a 200-branch bank. The opportunity to buy Economico suited our strategy perfectly," he said.
The Economico deal, struck for an undisclosed amount, catapulted Excel from 40th to 15 in the ranking of Brazil's banks.
Nasser changed the name to Banco Excel Economico and invested heavily in an image and a public relations drive.
The results are in the figures. Excel Economico ended 1996 with a 23.3 million real net profit, over 3.0 billion reais ($2.9 billion) in assets and a net worth of 530 million reais.
In the 10 months since the Economico acquisition, the number of Excel Economico clients has jumped to 700,000 current and savings account holders from 300,000.
Nasser says that explosive growth is explained by aggresive marketing, which includes 12 days of interest-free credit for overdrafts on current accounts.
Excel Economico has also launched a Mastercard that allows clients to walk into 140 cinemas without paying cash at the front box office.
These unconventional strategies are at the heart of Nasser's thinking. "We have to offer unique products, fast," he said. "That's what scares the competition."
THREE GENERATIONS IN THE BANKING BUSINESS
Nasser is a nephew of the legendary Edmond, Joseph and Moises Safra, a Jewish Syrian family whose banking empire stretches across Brazil, Europe, Israel and the United States.

He says he learned the business as a trainee at his uncle Edmond Safra's Republic National Bank of New York which he joined in 1966. Nasser said it was Edmond who taught him not to be afraid of breaking the rules.

He remembers how in the late 1960's The Republic National Bank of New York succeeded in attracting new business by giving away free television sets to every client who opened a savings account and kept it for two years.
"We were giving away 500 TV sets a day," he said.

In 1974, Nasser returned to Brazil. He worked for his uncles Joseph and Moises Safra at their well-established Banco Safra until he abruptly decided to leave in 1990, reportedly after a family disagreement.
Shortly before, Nasser admits to having lost at least $8 million in the much publicised June 1989 Brazilian stock market crash in which Lebanese mega-speculator Naji Nahas played a central role.
"It was the biggest hit I ever took," said Nasser.
With his father and his younger brother, Nasser founded a small investment bank that he called Excel Banco.
The new bank grew despite formidable difficulties.
The first was President Fernando Collor de Mello's draconian 1990 anti-inflation plan, which froze virtually all money in banks, where most cash had taken refuge from 80 percent a month inflation.
The second was when he spent 75 days in the hands of kidnappers.
"That was my toughest lesson yet. As time goes by, you try to forget, but you never forget," he said.
Nasser has also been investigated by the Brazilian Federal Police and the Central Bank for alleged illegal money remittances abroad, although no charges were ever filed against him.

Plans for the future include the establishment of an investment bank with his Swiss partner Union Bancaire Privee (UBP), which already owns 14 percent of Excel Economico's capital. Nasser also wants to increase business by moving into the booming insurance market.
Sitting in his executive suite at the top of the 19-floor Excel Economico building he speaks confidently of his bank's future.
"In this bank, the boss is the owner, so things get done."
He puffs on his cigar and adds:"We have built a bank to do banking in a non-traditional way." ($ = 1.049 Brazilian Reais)
